title: Silent japa

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri: the oldest mantra, asking the sun to light up our minds. Your line was light, illuminate the mind. Did you give the morning light a breath? Today, the mantra goes quiet. Day one hundred nine.

You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself. Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? The tradition noticed this long ago. Say a mantra out loud for long enough, and one day you catch it going on inside you while you're doing something else entirely. Nobody's saying it. It's just saying itself. There's a word for that.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?` → `NOBODY IS SAYING IT.`

segments.voice: First, the three ways of japa. Out loud, which you did with Hare Krishna, is called vachika, spoken. Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. And silent, only in the mind, is manasika, mental. Several old texts and teachers rank these, and they put the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, they say, the deeper it goes in. Not because out loud is wrong. Because silent japa has nowhere to hide. There's no sound to lean on. Just you and the mantra. And then there's a fourth thing, which isn't really a way of doing japa at all. It's called ajapa. The a at the front means not. Ajapa: not-repeating. The mantra that happens without anyone doing it. The yoga traditions describe it with the breath. Listen to your breathing. Some teachers say the in-breath makes a soft sound like so, and the out-breath a sound like ham. So-ham. It's a Sanskrit phrase that means I am that. And the old texts say every living being repeats it, all day and all night, with every breath, without knowing, thousands of times a day. They call it the ajapa gayatri, the Gayatri that isn't said. You can't force ajapa. You can only notice it. The practice is to start silent japa, then gradually let go of saying it, and see if the breath carries it on. It says itself.
screen: `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, SILENT.` · `THE QUIETER, THE DEEPER.` · `AJAPA — NOT-REPEATING.` · `SO ON THE IN-BREATH, HAM ON THE OUT.` · then, large: `IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: silent japa, then letting go. Sit, and settle into your breath. Pick your mantra, the one that fits, or simply so-ham. Say it silently: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out. No lips, no whisper. Just inside. After a while, stop saying it on purpose. Just listen to the breath, and see if you can still hear the so and the ham in it. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently. Back and forth. The bell holds the time.
Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.
Your line: it says itself. Today, once in a quiet minute, listen for so-ham in your own breath, or your mantra, running underneath what you're doing. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

trapdoor: what you thought: silent japa means saying it in your head.
what it means: past saying it at all: ajapa, the mantra the breath carries on its own, so on the way in, ham on the way out.
what a scholar hears: the ajapa gayatri of hamsa in texts like the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, with the traditional count of 21,600 breaths a day; the ranking of vachika, upamshu and manasika japa.

sources.ref: Dhyanabindu Upanishad (hamsa, the ajapa gayatri, 21,600 breaths)
the three kinds of japa (vachika, upamshu, manasika), e.g. Manusmriti 2.85 and later mantra texts

notes: Ajapa gayatri / hamsa and the count of 21,600 breaths per day: in the Dhyanabindu Upanishad and hatha/tantra texts; the script says 'thousands of times a day' and puts 21,600 only in the trapdoor. Confirm citation.
Which sound goes with which breath: some teach so on the in-breath and ham on the out (so-ham); others the reverse (ham-sa). Script says 'some teachers say'. Confirm.
Ranking of the three kinds of japa: Manusmriti 2.85 ranks muttered (upamshu) above ritual and mental higher still; later texts rank vachika < upamshu < manasika. Confirm.
